framework: AP Music Theory Course and Exam Description (effective fall 2026)
subject: Music Theory

source.licence: © College Board; structure + our own wording only

outcomes.text: Identify pitches on the staff in treble, bass and C clefs, whether heard or notated.
Read pitch from position on the staff and clef, and know octaves and accidentals.
Recognize enharmonic equivalents, the same pitch spelled differently.
Spot pitch differences between a notated score and what is performed.
Know that performed pitches should match the score except where improvisation or ornament is allowed.
Sight-sing the pitches and rhythms of a notated melody in treble or bass clef.
Sing notated pitches accurately, keeping the same intervals even if transposed.
Know a sight-singing is partly right if it keeps the tonic or the correct contour.
Hold each note for its full length, especially at cadences.
Identify note and rest values in performed and notated music.
Know that values show duration, extended by ties and single or double dots.
Identify half and whole steps in performed and notated music.
Know pitch patterns start with the half step and the whole step (two half steps).
Identify major scales in performed and notated music.
Build major and minor scales from set patterns of whole and half steps.
Name a pitch's function relative to the tonic using scale degree names or numbers.
Know the scale degree names from tonic to leading tone, and their numbers.
Identify major keys and key signatures in notated music.
Understand that music built on a scale is in that key.
Know key signatures show a scale's sharps or flats; diatonic versus chromatic pitches.
Use the circle of fifths to see which keys are closely related.
Notate the pitches and rhythms of a performed melody in treble or bass clef.
Take melodic dictation by hearing pitches against the tonic, spelling them in key and placing the octave.
Describe beat division and meter type in performed and notated music.
Understand meter as layered pulses: beat, division and measure.
Tell simple meter (beat splits in two) from compound meter (beat splits in three).
Describe the meter type in performed and notated music.
Name meters by division and beat grouping: simple or compound, duple, triple or quadruple.
Describe the time signature in performed and notated music.
Read the upper and lower numbers of a time signature to find beats, beat value and meter type.
Explain metrical accent: downbeat, strong and weak beats, and onbeat versus offbeat divisions.
Identify, notate and sight-sing rhythmic patterns in simple and compound meter.
Know the common ways rhythmic values fill a beat, and use named patterns such as dotted rhythms.
Beam and group notated rhythm so the beats stay clearly visible.
Spot rhythm differences between notated and performed music in one or two voices.
Know performed rhythm should match the score unless a style, such as swing, allows deviation.
Identify and apply tempo markings, including tempo adjustments, in performed and notated music.
Know Italian tempo terms from largo to prestissimo and metronome markings.
Know terms for speeding up, slowing down and flexible tempo, such as accelerando, ritardando and rubato.
Identify dynamics and changes in dynamics in performed and notated music.
Read dynamic marks from pp to ff, hairpins, crescendo, subito, and sforzando accents.
Identify articulation and changes in articulation in performed and notated music.
Read articulation marks: staccato, legato, slurs, accents and tremolo.
Sight-sing a notated melody while applying its dynamics, articulation and tempo.
Sing at sight with steady tempo and continuity, observing marked expression without hesitating.

topics.title: 2.1 Minor Scales: Natural, Harmonic, and Melodic

outcomes.text: Identify natural, harmonic and melodic minor scales in performed and notated music.
Know the harmonic and melodic minor are altered forms of natural minor.
Identify and notate a relative key and its key signature.
Know relative keys share a key signature but have different tonics.
Identify minor and relative keys in performed and notated music.
Know a minor key shares its key signature with its relative major.
Use the term mode for major and minor, and recognize a change in mode.
Describe parallel, closely related and distantly related key relationships.
Know parallel keys share a tonic but differ in key signature.
Know closely related keys differ by at most one accidental.
Know distantly related keys differ by more than one accidental.
Identify chromatic, whole-tone and pentatonic scales in performed and notated music.
Know the notes of chromatic, whole-tone, and major and minor pentatonic scales.
Describe the size and quality of an interval in performed and notated music.
Name intervals by distance and quality: major, minor, perfect, diminished, augmented.
Tell harmonic from melodic intervals, and steps from leaps.
Tell consonant (stable) intervals from dissonant (unstable) ones.
Identify interval inversions and compound intervals in performed and notated music.
Invert intervals and know how sizes and qualities change; inversions sum to nine.
Know compound intervals add an octave to a simple interval and sound alike.
Find sounding pitches from notated pitches of a transposing instrument, given the transposition.
Know transposing instruments sound differently from written pitches, so scores need conversion.
Identify performance media and vocal and instrumental timbres in performed music.
Recognize standard ensembles, timbre, register and tessitura.
Know the instrument families and common members of each, plus groupings like rhythm section and continuo.
Identify features of melody in performed and notated music.
Know melody comes from pitch and rhythm together.
Know melodies draw on scales and modes and form motives and phrases.
Describe contour, conjunct versus disjunct motion, register and range.
Define a motive as a small recurring musical idea that can be developed.
Tell syllabic text setting from melismatic text setting.
Transpose a melody to a new pitch level while keeping its intervals and rhythm.
Identify texture types in performed and notated music.
Understand texture as how musical components combine, shaped by timbre, density and range.
Name texture types: monophony, homophony, polyphony, heterophony, plus canon and call-and-response.
Identify texture devices in performed and notated music.
Recognize devices such as Alberti bass, walking bass, imitation, countermelody, ostinato and tutti.
Identify rhythmic devices in performed and notated music.
Recognize syncopation, cross-rhythm and hemiola.
Recognize agogic accent, anacrusis and fermata.
Identify irregular beat division or grouping in performed and notated music.
Recognize borrowed divisions such as triplets and duplets and irregular divisions.
Tell symmetrical from asymmetrical meters and recognize changing or mixed meter.
Describe the quality of a chord in performed and notated music.
Know chords have three or more pitches; triads and seventh chords are stacked thirds.
Name chord members: root, third, fifth and seventh.
Classify triads as major, minor, diminished or augmented by their intervals.
Identify chords with letters and Roman or Arabic numerals showing root, quality and bass.
Label diatonic chords with Roman numerals, upper or lower case, and scale degree names.
Identify root position and inversions, using figured bass numerals and letter-name chord labels.
Use Roman numerals to show the harmonic progression implied by a figured bass.
Read figured bass numerals as intervals above the bass that imply chords.
Read slashes, plus signs and lone accidentals in figured bass as raised pitches.
Describe the quality of a seventh chord in performed and notated music.
Name the five common seventh chord qualities, including dominant seventh and half- and fully-diminished.
Recognize the chordal seventh as a chordal dissonance that needs to resolve.
Identify seventh chords with Roman and Arabic numerals showing root, quality and bass.
Know seventh chords can sit in third inversion with the seventh in the bass.

units.title: Unit 4: Harmony and Voice Leading I

outcomes.text: Compose a bass line for a given soprano, following 18th-century harmonic norms.
Imply plausible harmonies with a bass line, using tonic, supertonic, subdominant and dominant, and valid repeats.
Use Roman and Arabic numerals to label the chords a bass line implies.
Analyze bass-line progressions so that every given note is explained by the chords.
Notate soprano and bass pitches and rhythms of a performed harmonic progression.
Take outer-voice dictation: bass octave displacement is tolerated, soprano octave is not.
Use soprano and bass to identify the chords and show them in Roman numeral analysis.
Compose a bass line against a soprano following 18th-century melodic procedures.
Balance up and down motion and steps and leaps for melodic interest in the bass.
Know which bass leaps are allowed and how to follow octave leaps.
Know when repeated bass notes are acceptable.
Compose the rhythm of a bass line in the style of an 18th-century chorale.
Use mostly quarter notes in the bass, with occasional half and eighth notes.
Identify the beginnings, ends and lengths of phrases in performed and notated music.
Understand phrases as complete utterances ending in a cadence, usually four or eight measures.
Imply an appropriate cadence at each phrase ending in a bass line, finishing with a perfect authentic cadence.
Identify and apply 18th-century voice leading through analysis, error detection, writing and listening.
Understand voice leading as the smooth, independent movement of parts with correct spelling, spacing and doubling.
Name the four kinds of motion: parallel, similar, oblique and contrary.
Follow voice-leading rules: mostly steps, common tones, no voice crossing, no parallel fifths or octaves, leading tone resolves.
Apply voice-leading conventions to outer voices, avoiding cross relations and unresolved leading tones.
Describe the number of lines and each line's position among the lines in a passage.
Name lines as soprano, alto, tenor and bass, the usual SATB four-voice texture.
Tell close position from open position spacing.
Apply 18th-century chord spelling and doubling by analysis, error detection and writing.
Spell every chord correctly, with needed accidentals, in a realized Roman-numeral or figured bass.
Double chord members by convention: the root first, never the leading tone or seventh.
Spell inverted triads completely.
Apply 18th-century chord voicing and spacing by analysis, error detection and writing.
Vary the motion between outer voices and avoid more than three consecutive thirds or sixths.
Avoid rising unequal fifths, hidden fifths and octaves, and overlapping voices.
Know chords can be voiced in many arrangements within each part's range.
Keep adjacent upper voices within an octave of each other.
Apply spelling, doubling, spacing and voice-leading rules to progressions with first-inversion chords.
Follow normal voice-leading rules when writing first-inversion triads.

topics.title: 4.3 Harmonic Progression, Functional Harmony, and Cadences

outcomes.text: Identify and describe harmonic function within a chord progression.
Define tonal music as pitches organized around a tonic, as in common-practice style.
Describe a harmonic progression as a chord sequence, written in Roman numerals with inversions.
Describe harmonic rhythm as the rate at which chords change.
Assign each chord a tonic, dominant or predominant function.
Know tonic-dominant-tonic as the basic progression that establishes a key.
Distinguish normative chord successions from retrogressions such as V to IV.
Know predominant chords expand the pattern into tonic-predominant-dominant-tonic.
Know IV and ii typically precede the dominant as predominant harmonies.
Identify cadence types in performed and notated music.
Tell conclusive cadences (perfect authentic, plagal) from inconclusive ones (half, imperfect authentic, deceptive).
Recognize special labeled progressions such as the Picardy third.
Know plagal and Phrygian half cadences use predominant function and deceptive cadences substitute for tonic.
Follow normal conventions for chordal sevenths in four-voice writing.
Approach chordal sevenths by common tone or step, and sometimes by a leap of a third.
Resolve chordal sevenths down by step, with known exceptions.
Omit the fifth of a root-position dominant seventh when helpful, doubling the root.
Use leading-tone seventh chords to substitute for V or to prolong the tonic.

topics.title: 4.5 Voice Leading with Seventh Chords in Inversion

outcomes.text: Connect inverted seventh chords smoothly with a stepwise bass.
Spell inverted seventh chords completely and resolve undoubled tendency tones.
Resolve sevenths in inverted chords downward by step, noting exceptions in V4/3 and ii7 patterns.

units.title: Unit 5: Harmony and Voice Leading II

outcomes.text: Identify and describe harmonic function and progression in performed and notated music.
Know vi (VI) can substitute for tonic or act as a weak predominant.
Recognize the deceptive progression, dominant to a non-tonic chord, usually vi.
Know the mediant triad is rare in 18th-century style; III in minor represents the relative major.
Identify the 6/4 chord type used in notated music.
Know 6/4 chords appear only as cadential, neighboring/pedal, passing or arpeggiated patterns.
Know the cadential 6/4 embellishes the dominant and sits on a stronger beat.
Apply 18th-century voice leading of cadential 6/4 chords by analysis, error detection and writing.
Resolve the sixth and fourth above the bass down by step in a cadential 6/4.
Read figures such as 6-5 over 4-3 as reminders of cadential 6/4 voice leading.
Describe the type of 6/4 chord used in notated music.
Describe the neighboring (pedal) 6/4 on a weak beat over a stationary bass.
Describe the passing 6/4 over a bass passing tone, on a weak beat.
Describe the arpeggiated 6/4 from a bass arpeggio under static upper voices.
Apply voice leading for passing, pedal and arpeggiated 6/4 chords.
Double the fifth in a passing 6/4 and move all voices by step.
Embellish the third and fifth with upper neighbors over a stationary bass in a pedal 6/4.
Keep upper voices still while the bass arpeggiates in an arpeggiated 6/4.
Imply good chord progressions in a bass line, placing 6/4 chords correctly and avoiding poor successions.

units.title: Unit 6: Harmony and Voice Leading III

topics.title: 6.1 Embellishing Tones: Passing and Neighbor Tones

outcomes.text: Identify embellishing and nonharmonic tones in performed and notated music.
Define nonharmonic tones and classify them by approach, resolution and accented versus unaccented placement.
Know related terms: embellishment, ornament, trill, preparation, resolution.
Identify passing tones and upper and lower neighbor tones.
Compose a bass line with unaccented passing or neighbor tones in 18th-century style.
Use eighth-note embellishments to complement a stationary soprano, move in parallel thirds or sixths, or exchange voices.

topics.title: 6.3 Anticipations, Escape Tones, Appoggiaturas, and Pedal Points

outcomes.text: Identify anticipations, escape tones, appoggiaturas and pedal points.
Identify suspensions, rearticulated suspensions, chains and upward-resolving suspensions.
Notate embellishing tones indicated in a figured bass or Roman numeral progression.
Read numerals such as 4-3 to show nonharmonic tones like suspensions.
Identify motives and melodic and rhythmic procedures applied to them.
Recognize motives, fragmentation, literal and sequential repetition.
Identify and apply melodic procedures in performed and notated music.
Apply transformations such as augmentation, melodic inversion and retrograde.
Identify and apply procedures that transform rhythmic patterns.
Transform rhythms by augmentation and diminution.
Define melodic sequence as repeated transpositions of a segment at a constant interval.
Identify and apply harmonic sequences in performed and notated music.
Define harmonic sequence as a chord segment repeated at a constant transposition, sometimes with melodic sequence.

units.title: Unit 7: Harmony and Voice Leading IV

outcomes.text: Identify and describe tonicization in performed and notated music.
Define tonicization as a brief local tonic that does not change the main key.
Tonicize a chord with its secondary dominant, as in V/V, using accidentals.
Part-write secondary dominants following dominant doubling and voice-leading rules.
Recognize chromatic pitches, such as raised 4 going to 5, that suggest tonicization.
Use secondary leading-tone triads and sevenths to tonicize major or minor triads.
Part-write secondary leading-tone chords with normal leading-tone doubling and seventh resolution.
Identify modes in performed and notated music.
Name the modes: Ionian, Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Aeolian and Locrian.
Describe melodic relationships between phrases in performed and notated music.
Label phrase relationships with letters such as a a, a a' and a b.
Identify periods in performed and notated music.
Describe periods as antecedent and consequent phrases, parallel or contrasting.
Identify common sections in performed and notated music.
Recognize introduction, interlude, bridge, verse, refrain, chorus, coda and codetta.
